text: Doris "Granny D" Haddock, born Ethel Doris Rollins on January 24, 1910, in Laconia, New Hampshire, was an American political activist from New Hampshire. She attended Emerson College in Boston for three years before being expelled due to the policy that students could not marry at the time; she was later awarded an honorary degree in 2000. The daughter of Ethel and Carl Rollins, she married James Haddock and had a daughter, Betty, and a son, James Jr. She worked during the Great Depression as an executive secretary at the BeeBee Shoe factory in Manchester, New Hampshire, for twenty years and retired to Dublin, New Hampshire, in 1972. Her husband later died after a ten-year battle with Alzheimer's disease, and at the same time, her best friend passed away. During her 1999 walk across the United States, the hat she wore belonged to her best friend. Haddock had eight grandchildren: Heidi, Gillian, David Bradley, William, Alice, Joseph, Lawrence, and Raphael, and 16 great-grandchildren: Kyle, David, Jennie, Kendall, Peyton, Matthew, Richard, Grace, Justin, William, James, Beatrix, Tucker, Mathilda, Parker, and Clay. In 1960, she and her husband campaigned against planned hydrogen bomb testing in Alaska that threatened an Inuit fishing village at Point Hope. After Senator efforts to eliminate soft money failed in 1995, Haddock became increasingly involved in campaign finance reform and led a petition movement. On January 1, 1999, at age 88, she began a walk across the continental United States, starting in southern California at the Rose Bowl Tournament of Roses Parade and ending in Washington, D.C. on February 29, 2000, at age 90, covering more than 3,200 miles (5,100 km) over 14 months. She walked approximately ten miles each day, passing through California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky, Ohio, West Virginia, Maryland, Virginia, and the District of Columbia, making speeches along the way. The walk attracted significant media attention, and when she arrived in Washington, D.C., she was greeted by a crowd of 2,200 people. On the final day, several dozen members of Congress walked with her from Arlington National Cemetery to the Capitol on the National Mall. A film titled "Granny D Goes to Washington," directed by Alidra Solday, documented her journey and aired on PBS stations from 2006 to 2008. In the 2000 presidential election, she endorsed Green Party candidate Ralph Nader. She worked with state representative Betty Hall on campaign finance reform. On April 21, 2000, at age 90, she and 31 others were arrested for reading the Declaration of Independence in the U.S. Capitol, charged with demonstrating, though the assembly was peaceful. She pleaded guilty and stated that her purpose was to highlight the need for campaign finance reform, saying, "I was reading from the Declaration of Independence to make the point that we must declare our independence from the corrupting bonds of big money in our election campaigns," and added, "If it is a crime to read the Declaration of Independence in our great hall, then I am guilty." The judge sentenced her and her companions to time served and a $10 administrative fee. Haddock co-authored several books with Dennis Burke: Granny D: Walking Across America in My Ninetieth Year (Villard, 2001), Granny D: You're Never Too Old to Raise a Little Hell (Villard, 2003), and Granny D's American Century (University Press of New England, 2012). She received an honorary degree from Franklin Pierce College on October 21, 2002, and delivered the commencement speech at Hampshire College in 2005. In 2004, she ran as a Democratic challenger to incumbent Republican Judd Gregg in the U.S. Senate election in New Hampshire at age 94, becoming one of the oldest major-party candidates to run for the Senate. True to her "clean elections" ideals, she funded her campaign with only modest private-citizen donations and captured approximately 34 percent of the vote (221,549), losing to Gregg, who won about 66 percent (434,847). In 2007, HBO released a documentary, Run Granny Run, about her 2004 Senate campaign. In 2009, she founded the Coalition for Open Democracy. She remained politically active until her death and celebrated her 98th, 99th, and 100th birthdays by lobbying for campaign finance reform at the New Hampshire State House. She celebrated her 100th birthday on January 24, 2010, and died six weeks later on March 9, 2010, at her son's home in Dublin, New Hampshire, following a respiratory illness. On August 19, 2004, her request to change her middle name to "Granny D" was officially granted by Judge John Maher at the Cheshire County probate court. She was a life-long member of the United Methodist Church. In 2000, she received a special Martin Luther King Award from the Manchester, New Hampshire-based Martin Luther King Coalition and was the keynote speaker at that year's Martin Luther King Day Community Celebration in Manchester.
